newsitem.title: UK: HORSE RACING-CARSON HANGS UP HIS RIDING BOOTS.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-CARSON HANGS UP HIS RIDING BOOTS.

text.p: Five times champion jockey Willie Carson, whose liver was split in a racecourse accident last September, has confirmed he is retiring after 35 years in the saddle.
Carson, whose 3,500 winners include four triumphs in the Epsom Derby, said: "I made the final decision on Saturday. I am getting old and my body is wearing out."
The ebullient Scotsman, whose pumping action galvanised so many champions, had won 17 classics and was booked to ride Bahhare, the 7-2 favourite for the 2,000 Guineas in May.

But he clearly felt he was losing the fight back to fitness in a tough and unforgiving sport where he had rivalled the great Lester Piggott for longevity. Only Piggott and Sir Gordon Richards had ridden more winners than Carson.

"I have ripped something in my back and it is giving me trouble. I had it last year before the accident and now it is back. It was the signal for me to quit," he told the News of the World tabloid which broke the story.
Carson, 54, won his first Epsom Derby in 1979 in spectacular fashion on Troy, who spreadeagled the field.
Another highlight for the flying Scot, known as "Wee Willie", was riding Queen Elizabeth's Dunfermline to victory in the Oaks in her Silver Jubilee year, 1977.
Carson, an inveterate joker with his trademark cackling giggle in post-race interviews, also singled out Minster Son's 1988 St Leger victory as another treasured memory. He bred the colt himself.
He was badly injured last September when Meshhed, in the colours of his retainer, Dubai's Sheikh Hamdam Al-Maktoum, lashed out in the paddock at Newbury racecourse.
One commentator quipped that Carson rose to glory "in a blaze of mediocrity." He finished last on his first ride in May 1959 and it took three years for him to boot home a winner.
But tenacity paid dividends for Carson who won his first classic -- on High Top -- and his first jockeys title in 1972. He has ridden a century of winners 21 times in a season.

Carson's blunt-spoken autobiography revealed a darker side to his chirpy image but punters loved what they saw -- a driven figure pumping furiously away in the saddle, squeezing every last bit out of his mounts with his furious will to win.
Fellow champion Pat Eddery once said of Carson: "If they keep oiling him, he'll go on for ever."
On Sunday the oil finally ran out in the Carson engine.
